Registered Office: Charles House, 108-110 Finchley Road, London NW3 5JJ July 2012 Vol 40 No 1 ### Reuters’ July 2012 Base Metals poll – lowering the sights The Reuters’ mid-year poll this year shows average cash copper price forecasts of 363¢/lb ($7,999/t) for 2012 and 376¢/lb (8,292/t) for 2013. The average for 2012 is virtually the same as the average price in the year to end-July and only very slightly above CRU’s forecast of 360¢/lb ($7,938/t, from our July 2012 Quarterly). For 2013, CRU’s forecast is for a stronger rise in the price than the poll suggests, as we are forecasting an average price of 386¢/lb ($8,506/t), which is 10¢/lb above the poll average. When looking at the market balance, the participants in the poll are almost in unanimous agreement that the market is in deficit in 2012, with an annual average of 191,000t for the whole year. CRU is at the higher end of the scale for deficits, anticipating a 480,000t shortfall of production to consumption in 2012. We are nearer the average of the poll for 2013, with our surplus of 25,000t vs. the poll’s average surplus of 19,000t.  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com
www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES July 2012 2 ### Forecasts across the LME complex for 2012 are in line with year-to-date average In the January 2011 Reuters’ poll of base metals analysts the fore

cast prices across all LME metals were all above the actual out turn prices for the year. The metal with the largest error was zinc. The average forecast was for 110¢/lb but in the end the price averaged only 99.4¢/lb, or 9.8% below. At the other extreme, the average aluminium price forecast was off by only 1.5% from the actual. Forecasts from the latest poll for 2012 suggest that all prices will end the year with an annual average that will be below 2011 levels. In addition, the forecasts across all metals are not much different from the average prices from January through to the end of July this year. The difference between the average forecast and the actual average for the first seven months of the year ranges from 1.3% below for tin to 1.1% above for lead. In 2013, the average forecasts for all LME metals are for a rise in the price, ranging from 4-10%. However, the result is that no metal is forecast to end 2013 with an average price that exceeds the average recorded in 2011. |Consensus LME

### Copper price expected to see modest rise over the remainder of 2012… The average forecast of the cash copper price for 2012 by the 31 analysts in the Reuters’ poll is

363¢/lb ($7,998/t), which is virtually the same as the average LME cash copper price for the January-July period (364¢/lb). Therefore, the participants are not expecting to see very strong price movement over the remainder of 2012. However, since the beginning of June, the price has traded in the $7,200-$7,800/t range, and the implication therefore is that the analysts expect to see the price rise through to the end of the year. In order to hit the average, prices would have to average 361¢/lb ($7,968/t) for the five months from August to December. Among the 31 analysts, none are forecasting an average price above the 2011 average of 400¢/lb ($8,811/t). The highest forecast comes from CESCO at 390¢/lb ($8,598/t). In order for this forecast to be achieved the price would have to average 427¢/lb ($9,407/t) over the five months August to December. At the other end of the spectrum, the lowest forecast value is 343¢/lb ($7,551/t) from the Central Bank of Montenegro. While this price in within the current trading range, it implies an average monthly price for the remaining 5 months of the year of just 313¢/lb ($6,893/t). There is very little skew to the range of forecasts, as there are roughly equal numbers of observations above and below the average. The range of forecasts is also quite narrow, with the highest forecast only 14% above the lowest. By comparison, the forecasts at the beginning of 2011, when prices were rising strongly, showed a range in which the high was 41% above the low (discounting an outlier of 300¢/lb, which is 72% below the high!). For comparison, CRU’s forecast in our July Quarterly is for a 2012 average price of 360¢/lb ($7,938/t), which places us marginally below the average of the other analysts.  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES July 2012 4 |Analysts' forecasts of cash copper prices, 2012 and

### …with further small rise foreseen in 2013 The average copper price forecast for 2013 is 376¢/lb (8,292/t), up by only 4% on the 2012 forecast level. There are 8 analysts out of 31 that expect the copper price to fall in 2013. UBS is the most bearish, expecting the price to decline by 31% from a relatively low forecast of 351¢/lb (7,740/t) for 2012 to 320¢/lb ($7,055/t), which is the lowest forecast for next year. This would be the lowest annual average price since 2009 and below the averages for 2006-2008. On the other hand, Standard Chartered is forecasting the highest increase for 2013. This 19% y-o-y growth takes its already bullish 2012 forecast of 381¢/lb ($8,404/t) and boosts it to 454¢/lb ($10,000/t), which not surprisingly is the highest 2013 forecast in the group. For comparison, CRU’s forecast in our July Quarterly is for a 2013 average price of 386¢/lb ($8,506/t) or 10¢/lb above the poll mean. ### Balances show an almost universal expectation of a deficit in 2012… The forecast for the market balance in 2012 is, on the face of it, somewhat at odds with the subdued forecasts for the price. There were 18 analysts who provided a forecast of the copper market balance. SocGen is the only participant to have submitted a forecast of a surplus for this year, namely 70,000t. All other analysts are anticipating a deficit, with the forecasts ranging from 76,000t from Standard Bank to 540,000t from Deutsche Bank. In 2012, the analysts’ average forecast deficit is 191,000t, which given the relatively low stock levels on exchanges could be construed as a sign that the price should be higher. However, CRU forecasts a deficit for 2012 of 480,000t, or at the high end of the poll range and a price near the average. We justify this  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES July 2012 6 because of the extreme uncertainty affecting all financial markets, which has prompted investors to keep large parts of their holdings in cash and as a result this weighs on commodity prices. ### …and a more mixed picture of a balanced market in 2013 For 2013, a total of 17 analysts submitted forecasts, with seven continuing to expect the market to be in deficit but to a lesser extent than in 2012 at an average of 152,000t. CESCO is

expecting the largest deficit of 250,000t. A further seven analysts expect the market to be in significant surplus in 2013, ranging up to 270,000t from 2012’s most bearish SocGen. These seven forecasts average 189,000t. The remaining three analysts forecast the market to be in balance. Overall, the average is 18,000t, or for a balanced market. On a cumulative basis, over the next two years the implied change in copper stocks ranges from a drawdown of 450,000t (CESCO) to a build of 340,000t (SocGen), with a cumulative average drawdown of 173,000t. This compares to CRU’s July forecast of a cumulative deficit over the next two years of over 450,000t. In fact, we expect a tighter market than the analysts’ average for 2012 and an almost balanced market in 2013. Our relatively high price forecast for 2013 is supported by this cumulative drawdown of stocks, especially as we see the market in 2013 being in balance in the year as a whole, but with a deficit in H1 and a surplus in H2. The deficit in H1 will draw stocks down towards, but not quite reaching, the critically low levels that would push prices up towards $10,000/t. The number of participants has fallen sharply over the past 18 months. In the January 2011 poll, there were 50 submissions from analysts that provided a copper price forecast. In the July 2011 poll this shrank to only 40 participants, a 20% reduction. In the latest poll the number has shrunk even further to only 31, a further 22.5% decline.

Why has there been such a reduction in participation?  One reason could be that some companies no longer wish to publicise their price forecasts.  For example, CRU has never participated because the timing of the polls would mean that our clients who take our Quarterly services would see our price forecasts in January and July in the poll before they receive their Quarterly. 

However, another reason for the reduction is that the financial sector has suffered precipitous declines in revenue in the last year or so.  The sector recovered in 2010 due to the broader economic recovery but also the record low interest rate environment adopted by central banks.  Since then, though, the economy in developed markets has slowed and policy interest rates at central banks have reached close to zero.  So monetary policy cannot help to offset difficult market conditions and revenue has declined at many financial service firms by 20-30%.  As a result, some financial service firms have reduced coverage of base metals and, as a result, may no longer be in a position to provide independent price forecasts.  We will have to wait until the January 2013 poll to see whether more firms submit forecasts or if this reduction in participation is a permanent one.
